title: SQL Day 4 — Aggregations, GROUP BY & KPI Analysis
description: Turn transaction rows into management KPIs using COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, GROUP BY, and HAVING.

topics.title: COUNT & COUNT DISTINCT
topics.business_skill: Measure transaction volume and unique business entities.

teaching.teacher: ## COUNT\nCOUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-null values; COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) counts unique customers.
teaching.explain: Choose the counting grain first: rows, populated values, or unique entities.
teaching.detailedlearning: A business request for orders, customers, products, or transactions implies a different counting unit.
teaching.expose: Never report a count until you can state exactly what one counted row represents.
teaching.example: SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_rows, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS unique_customers FROM orders;
teaching.business_question: The sales director wants total transaction rows and unique customers.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_rows, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS unique_customers FROM orders;

questions.scenario: Management wants the number of sales transactions.
questions.request: Return the total number of order records.

questions.scenario: The team wants the active customer population represented in the dataset.
questions.request: Return the number of distinct customer IDs.

questions.scenario: Finance is checking whether order volume and customer volume are being confused.
questions.request: Return both total order rows and distinct customers in one result.
questions.validation: Two separate counts at different grains.

teaching.teacher: ## Numeric aggregates\nSUM totals a measure, AVG calculates the arithmetic mean, MIN finds the smallest value, and MAX finds the largest.
teaching.explain: Aggregates collapse many rows into one summary unless a grouping column is included.
teaching.detailedlearning: Use meaningful aliases and keep the measure definition explicit.
teaching.expose: Averages can hide skew; use them deliberately rather than assuming they represent a typical transaction.
teaching.example: SELECT SUM(sales) AS total_sales, AVG(sales) AS avg_sales, MIN(sales) AS min_sales, MAX(sales) AS max_sales FROM orders;
teaching.business_question: The CFO wants a basic sales KPI snapshot.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT SUM(sales) AS total_sales, AVG(sales) AS avg_sales, MIN(sales) AS min_sales, MAX(sales) AS max_sales FROM orders;

questions.scenario: Finance needs the total sales value.
The manager wants to understand order-value spread.
questions.request: Return average, minimum, and maximum sales per order.

questions.scenario: The monthly review requires a compact sales KPI block.
questions.request: Return total sales, total profit, average sales, and maximum sales.

topics.title: GROUP BY — KPI by Business Dimension
topics.business_skill: Compare metrics across regions, categories, or segments.

teaching.teacher: ## GROUP BY\nGROUP BY creates one result group for each distinct combination of grouping columns.
teaching.explain: Every selected non-aggregated column must define the grouping grain.
teaching.detailedlearning: Think of GROUP BY as changing the question from 'What is the total?' to 'What is the total for each X?'.
teaching.expose: State the dimension before writing the aggregate.
teaching.example: SELECT region, SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY region;
teaching.business_question: The regional director wants sales by region.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT region, SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY region;

questions.request: Return total sales for each region.

questions.scenario: The category team wants category-level profitability.
questions.request: Return total sales and total profit for each category.

questions.scenario: The director wants segment performance by region.
questions.request: Return region, segment, total sales, and total profit for each region-segment combination.

teaching.teacher: ## HAVING\nHAVING filters groups after aggregation; WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation.
teaching.explain: Use WHERE for source-row conditions and HAVING for conditions on aggregate results.
teaching.detailedlearning: If the condition contains SUM, COUNT, AVG, MIN, or MAX, HAVING is usually the relevant clause.
teaching.expose: Do not replace HAVING with WHERE when the business rule is about a group KPI.
teaching.example: SELECT region, SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY region HAVING SUM(sales) >= 10000;
teaching.business_question: The director wants only regions with at least 10,000 in sales.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT region, SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY region HAVING SUM(sales) >= 10000;

questions.scenario: Only regions above a sales threshold should appear.
questions.request: Return regions whose total sales are at least 10,000.

questions.scenario: Finance wants categories with negative aggregate profit.
questions.request: Return categories whose total profit is below zero.

questions.scenario: Management wants customer accounts generating more than 5,000 in sales.
questions.request: Return customer IDs with total sales above 5,000.

topics.title: Business KPI Summary
topics.business_skill: Combine multiple aggregates into a management-ready result.

teaching.teacher: ## KPI summary\nA useful management query combines the required measures at the requested grain and gives each output a clear name.
teaching.explain: Start with grain, then measures, then filters, then ordering.
teaching.detailedlearning: Avoid returning unnecessary columns because every extra dimension can change the aggregation grain.
teaching.expose: A technically valid query can still be a bad report if the grain is ambiguous.
teaching.example: SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(sales) AS sales, SUM(profit) AS profit FROM orders GROUP BY region;
teaching.business_question: The COO wants regional orders, sales, and profit.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(sales) AS sales, SUM(profit) AS profit FROM orders GROUP BY region;

questions.scenario: Leadership wants a regional KPI table.
questions.request: Return region, order count, sales, and profit.

questions.scenario: The manager wants category performance in one view.
questions.request: Return category, order count, total sales, and average discount.

questions.scenario: A review pack needs region-level profitability and volume.
questions.request: Return region, distinct customers, order count, sales, profit, and average discount.
